PART SEVEN
Guilt & Temptation
CHAPTER 61
When You Feel Guilty
Before you apologize, ask what you are apologizing for. A
promise you broke may need acknowledging. Someone's
disappointment with a boundary you kept may need a different
response. Guilt can feel urgent in either situation, even when
your responsibility is not yet clear.
You may also feel guilty about something another person did to
you. The feeling alone cannot tell you whose responsibility it
was.
Before treating it as a verdict, consider the concern itself. What
happened? What choice did you make? What have you been told
you should feel responsible for?
Give the concern a truthful description
There may be a particular act to name: a promise you broke or a
confidence you shared. Speak about that act before God plainly.
You can acknowledge its seriousness without deciding that your
whole life has become worthless.
If someone was harmed, consider what repair is possible. The
chapter on asking for forgiveness gives more attention to an
apology and its practical commitments. Here, begin by

300
identifying what needs addressing, including any advice needed
before making contact.
Other situations require a different response. Refusing an
unreasonable demand can feel wrong if you are accustomed to
making everyone comfortable. Being mistreated can leave you
carrying the explanation the person who harmed you supplied.
Their accusation deserves examination; it is not automatically
an accurate account of your conduct.
You might need a careful conversation with someone
trustworthy to distinguish these things. Choose someone who
can hear the facts without either excusing a real wrong or
assigning you responsibility for another person's choices. If
abuse is involved, seek support that understands it.
Peter is given work to do again
Luke 22:54–62; John 21:12–19
On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter denied knowing Him
three times. When the rooster crowed, Peter remembered what
Jesus had told him. He went out and wept bitterly.
After the resurrection, Jesus shared breakfast with the disciples
by the sea. When they had eaten, He asked Peter whether he
loved Him. The question came three times, and each answer was
followed by a responsibility: feed His lambs, shepherd His
sheep, feed His sheep. Jesus then spoke about Peter's future and
told him to follow Him.
Peter's failure was real, and so was the relationship in which
Jesus now addressed him. He was entrusted with care for others.
The conversation concerned love and following Jesus after a
denial that neither of them needed explained away.
Your circumstances will differ from Peter's calling. Still, his
restoration gives a Christian reason to bring failure to Christ
with hope. Repentance can lead into a changed life, including
responsibilities you can take up again with care.

301
Where another person has been hurt, their trust remains their
decision. Peter's commission cannot be used to demand that
someone immediately restore a role or access you lost. Attend to
your responsibility and allow their response to be their own.
Mercy that takes wrongdoing seriously
As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our
transgressions from us.
Psalm 103:12, Berean Standard Bible
The psalm praises God's compassion and forgiveness. It speaks
to the burden of actual transgression. You can confess what is
yours to confess and receive mercy without minimizing the
wrong.
Isaiah 1:16–18 joins the promise of cleansing with a call to stop
doing evil, seek justice, and defend people who are being
oppressed. Forgiveness is held alongside a changed response to
others. It does not require you to remain in an endless account of
your unworthiness.
In 2 Corinthians 7:8–11, Paul considers the sorrow his letter
caused and the repentance that followed. The passage directs
attention to what the sorrow produced. It should not be turned
into a requirement that every regret disappear or into a
judgment that someone with persistent distress must be
refusing God.
Ask what faithful action is called for now. It may be an
acknowledgment, practical repair, or a change in a recurring
decision. If there is no actual wrong to confess, the next need
may be help understanding why you feel responsible.

302
When certainty keeps slipping away
There is a difference between facing a concern and spending
hours trying to obtain complete certainty that you have done
nothing wrong. If checking, repeated confession, or asking
others for reassurance gives only brief relief and takes over your
life, tell a mental health professional. Religious and moral
worries can occur within OCD, sometimes called scrupulosity;
an assessment can help identify appropriate care.
An assessment considers the distressing pattern; having a
difficult conscience does not, by itself, establish an illness. A
faith leader who understands the concern can support
treatment while respecting your beliefs.
If someone you care about feels guilty
Ask what happened before offering a verdict. Help them name a
specific responsibility where one exists. Do not add accusations,
press for private details, or make humiliation part of an apology.
If they have been harmed, keep responsibility with the person
who chose to harm them. If they repeatedly ask the same moral
question and remain distressed, encourage suitable professional
help rather than trying to settle each new doubt yourself.
Pause and reflect
Does this concern identify a particular action, someone else's
accusation, or uncertainty that needs support?
What response would address the facts without turning the
whole of your life into a trial?

303
A prayer
Father, help me see what is mine to acknowledge. Give me courage to
confess a real wrong and wisdom about repairing it. Where I have
accepted blame that belongs elsewhere, help me understand the
truth. Let Your mercy shape what I do next, and guide me toward
help where guilt has become difficult to untangle. In Jesus' name,
amen.
For further reading: Psalm 103:8–14; Isaiah 1:16–18; Luke 22:54–62; John 21:12–19; 2
Corinthians 7:8–11; 1 John 1:5–9.
Read also:
• Asking for Forgiveness (p. 163), for an apology and the repair it requires.
• When You Cannot Forgive Yourself (p. 313), if acknowledged wrongdoing keeps
becoming self-punishment.
• When You Feel Ashamed (p. 43), if the feeling has become a judgment about your
whole self.
